title: Advanced Index Selection Lab
description: Choose advanced index structures through B+ tree fan-out, composite key access, skip scan limits, and engine-specific bitmap, spatial, and full-text labs.

questions.question_text: What is B+ tree fan-out?
options: The number of child routes in an internal node
questions.explanation: Fan-out describes routing capacity at an internal tree node.

questions.question_text: Why can narrow routing keys help tree depth?
options: More entries can fit in comparable page space
They guarantee every query is covered
questions.explanation: Higher routing capacity can address more leaves with fewer levels.

questions.question_text: Is a page split automatically an index error?
options: No, it is normal structural maintenance
questions.explanation: Splits maintain the tree as pages fill.

questions.question_text: What is the leading component of (campus_id, event_date, event_id)?
questions.explanation: Declared order determines the leading key component.

questions.question_text: Which predicate naturally matches that leading tuple?
options: A campus equality and event date range
questions.explanation: Fixing the leading component supports a bounded following range.

questions.question_text: What must be checked before relying on skip scan?
options: Only that a trailing column exists
questions.explanation: Skip scan support and choice depend on capabilities and cost.

questions.question_text: What does index coverage depend on?
options: The values required by a particular query
questions.explanation: An index covers a query when required values are available from it.

questions.question_text: Does adding title to the projection potentially change access work?
options: No, all columns are always in every index
Only if the name is uppercase
Yes, it may require a row lookup
questions.explanation: The current index does not necessarily contain title.

questions.question_text: What does a bitmap represent conceptually?
options: A set of matching row positions
questions.explanation: Bits can represent membership of row positions in a match set.

questions.question_text: Is a persistent bitmap index the same as every bitmap scan operation?
questions.explanation: An execution technique and a persistent structure are different concepts.

questions.question_text: Does MySQL InnoDB offer every engine bitmap DDL feature?
options: Only if the key is BIGINT
questions.explanation: Specialized index syntax and support are engine specific.

questions.question_text: What should be fixed before tuning a spatial boundary query?
questions.explanation: Correct spatial meaning precedes physical optimization.

questions.question_text: Why may a spatial candidate search need an exact predicate afterward?
options: Every point is inside every polygon
A candidate region can be broader than the true geometry
questions.explanation: Candidate filtering need not settle exact spatial membership.

questions.question_text: Why is full text search different from generic substring matching?
questions.explanation: Terms, parsers, stopwords, and ranking affect full text results.

questions.question_text: What can affect a full text search for a short word?
questions.explanation: Short tokens may be handled according to parser rules.

questions.question_text: Does an index merge two events sharing the same date?
questions.explanation: Indexing does not remove logical row occurrences.

questions.question_text: What is a missing geometry not automatically equivalent to?
options: A real point at the origin
questions.explanation: NULL and a genuine coordinate have different meanings.

questions.question_text: Why compare write costs before adding another index?
options: Each maintained structure adds work and storage
Every index is free after creation
questions.explanation: Physical structures must be maintained with data changes.

questions.question_text: What makes equal-date event ordering stable?
questions.explanation: A unique tie breaker completes the requested order.

questions.question_text: What does a static structure diagram fail to prove?
options: Actual optimizer use and measured cost
questions.explanation: Physical performance requires actual engine evidence.

notes:
## Match a structure to an access pattern

A campus library supports exact loan lookups, searches within document text, and map searches for nearby facilities. Calling each requirement an indexing problem is accurate but incomplete. Different structures organize different kinds of search. A B+ tree is useful for ordered keys and ranges. Full text indexes support token based document retrieval. Spatial structures support geometric access patterns. Bitmap techniques combine sets of matching rows in certain engines and workloads. One index label cannot substitute for the actual comparison and result contract.

Begin with representative queries and writes. Record equality predicates, range boundaries, ordering, selected columns, and expected match counts. Note whether data changes frequently and whether many sessions write concurrently. An index that helps a mostly static analytical table can be unsuitable for a hot transactional table. Physical design is a workload decision supported by evidence, rather than a checklist requiring every known index type.

## Understand B+ tree fan-out

A B+ tree uses internal routing entries to reach leaf pages containing keys and associated row information. Fan-out is the number of child routes an internal node can hold. More usable entries per internal page can reduce the number of levels needed for a given population. Key width and entry overhead therefore matter alongside row count. A narrow key can allow more routing entries than a wide key under comparable page constraints.

Use a simplified numerical model to reason about scale. If an internal level can route to one hundred children, two routing levels can address about ten thousand leaf pages. This arithmetic ignores occupancy variation, metadata, and engine details. Its purpose is to show why trees remain shallow as data grows, not to predict the exact height of a real index. Inspect the installed engine's physical metadata when precise capacity matters.

Insertions can fill a leaf and require a split, distributing entries and updating the parent structure. A split is not automatically corruption or an error. It is normal maintenance of an ordered structure. However, insertion distribution and available page space affect how often maintenance occurs and what locality remains. Removing records and changing keys also create maintenance work. Read performance should be assessed alongside these write costs.

## Composite keys use an ordered tuple

A multicolumn B+ tree on campus_id, event_date, event_id orders tuples by the declared components. A predicate fixing campus_id and selecting an event_date interval naturally identifies a contiguous region in that key space. The trailing event_id can distinguish equal dates. Changing the column order changes the available leading search patterns, even though the same names appear in the definition.

```sql
CREATE TABLE campus_events (
 event_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
 campus_id INT NOT NULL,
 event_date DATE NOT NULL,
 title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
 INDEX ix_campus_date (campus_id,event_date,event_id)
);
SELECT event_id,event_date
FROM campus_events
WHERE campus_id=4
 AND event_date >= '2026-04-01'
 AND event_date < '2026-05-01'
ORDER BY event_date,event_id;
```

The requested result is one campus's April events in stable order. A predicate only on event_date does not specify the leading campus component. Some engines and situations support skip scan strategies that consider multiple leading values, but this is not equivalent to declaring that any trailing predicate gets the same direct range path. Eligibility, selectivity, and optimizer cost determine whether such a strategy is available and selected.

## Distinguish filtering, coverage, and ordering

An index can narrow candidates, provide projected values, or support an ordering requirement. These are related benefits but they are not interchangeable. The event index contains event_id and event_date, so the illustrated projection can be covered under suitable engine behavior. Adding title may require a row lookup. An index being present does not guarantee that the optimizer chooses it or avoids every sort.

A range condition can also limit how later key components help identify a single contiguous interval. Do not memorize a vague rule that every listed column is equally searchable in every query. Work through the ordered tuple and inspect the actual plan. Add only structures whose benefit is demonstrated against their storage and maintenance cost. Two nearly identical composite indexes may be partly redundant, but check their callers before removing either.

## Bitmap techniques are engine specific

A bitmap represents a set of matching row positions as bits. Combining bitmaps can support analytical predicates such as a collection of demographic categories. The physical cost depends on compression, row population, update behavior, and engine implementation. Low cardinality is a relevant clue, not a complete justification. A column with two values does not automatically require a bitmap index.

Distinguish a persistent bitmap index in engines that support it from a bitmap scan operation that combines other access paths at query time. They are not the same feature. MySQL InnoDB does not offer a general CREATE BITMAP INDEX counterpart to every other engine's syntax. Do not invent portable DDL from a conceptual category. Consult the target engine and version before proposing a specialized structure.

## Spatial and full text searches preserve their own semantics

A spatial index can help locate geometric candidates for spatial predicates. The geometry type, coordinate reference system, boundary behavior, and exact predicate remain essential to correctness. A candidate bounding region can be broader than the final exact geometric test. A map feature that means inside a campus boundary needs an explicit rule for points on the border; index availability does not decide that rule.

Full text indexing supports document search with tokenization and language related behavior that ordinary substring matching does not reproduce. Stopwords, token size, parser choice, and ranking affect results. A full text query and LIKE '%word%' should not be described as interchangeable solely because both look for text. Define whether the product needs token search, substring search, prefix search, or ranked retrieval, then select the correct mechanism.

NULL and duplicates still need a query contract. Several events can share one date and title; an index does not merge them. Missing geometry is not automatically a location at the origin. A missing document is not an empty meaningful text. Include these cases in semantic tests before interpreting a plan or comparing retrieval speed.

## Compare an index against a complete workload

Record the important queries that share the table before choosing a specialized structure. Include bulk imports, ordinary updates, and deletion of old data. A benchmark that times only a selective read misses the cost paid by every maintained write path. Keep a reviewed removal or rollback plan for an experiment that does not justify its overhead, and avoid changing several structures simultaneously when the goal is to identify which one caused an improvement.

## Worked lab: choose a multicolumn order

The task is to support one campus's events within a month, returning event identity and date. The proposed solution leads with campus_id, then event_date, and includes a tie breaker. Explain why a query spanning all campuses by date has a different leading access requirement. Compare the relevant plans instead of asserting that one composite order optimizes both workloads equally.

Add two events on the same day. The final ORDER BY event_date, event_id makes their display order explicit. Then request title and explain why coverage may change. This lab separates result ordering, selection, and projected values so a tuning discussion can identify exactly which benefit is sought.

## Worked lab: reject a mismatched specialized index

A document search product needs whole word ranking. The solution investigates the engine's full text feature and its tokenizer rather than adding a generic B+ tree on the entire document and promising substring acceleration. Test a stopword, a short token, punctuation, and an absent term. State which outcomes are semantic requirements and which depend on chosen configuration.

A map query is the second case. The solution first fixes coordinate conventions and the desired predicate, then investigates spatial indexing and exact boundary tests. Do not infer geographic distance from an arbitrary Cartesian example. These solved design labs need engine capabilities, plans, and representative datasets; output-only SQL grading would miss their physical purpose.

Use [Clustered Index](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/clustered-index) for row storage and [Function Based Index Concept](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/function-based-index-concept) for derived keys. This foundation introduces three advanced access concerns without claiming exhaustive index coverage or measured performance.
